name: Radiation converter
seoDesc: Radiation converter: work out dose in grays from the dose in rads and the dose in microsieverts. A free conversion calculator with the formula, units and…
summary: The Radiation converter turns the dose in rads and the dose in microsieverts into dose in grays. It suits a recipe, a shopping list, a travel plan or a form that asks for a unit you do not use. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Radiation converter calculator work?
sections.html:
The Radiation converter takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports dose in grays in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the dose in rads and the dose in microsieverts.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in rads. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in microsieverts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Radiation converter calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Dose in grays=dose in milligrays
Dose in millisieverts=dose in microsieverts
Dose in milligrays=dose in rads
Dose equivalent in roentgen equivalent man (rem)=dose in microsieverts

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in grays, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.
  • Shown in millisieverts, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in milligrays, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.
  • Shown in roentgen equivalent man (rem), and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Dose absorbed, opening in milligrays
  • Dose absorbed, opening in grays
  • Dose absorbed, opening in rads
  • Dose equivalent – sievert, opening in microsieverts
  • Dose equivalent – sievert, opening in millisieverts
  • Dose equivalent – sievert, opening in roentgen equivalent man (rem)

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Radiation converter earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Reading a recipe written in units you do not use
  • Filling in a form that asks for imperial or metric values
  • Checking a product listing against the measurements you work with
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the dose in rads and the dose in microsieverts — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Radiation converter, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Radiation converter calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns dose in grays, derived from the dose in rads and the dose in microsieverts. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Radiation converter calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the dose in rads and the dose in microsieverts, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter dose in milligrays in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Dose in milligrays opens in milligrays and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Radiation converter calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
